events.title: The secret pact of Philip V and Antiochus III
events.summary: After the death of Ptolemy IV left a child king in Egypt, Philip V and Antiochus III allegedly agreed to divide the Ptolemaic overseas possessions between them. Antiochus attacked Coele-Syria; Philip seized Ptolemaic and independent cities in the Aegean and the Straits.
events.detail: Polybius (15.20) condemns the pact as monstrous and calls the subsequent ruin of both kings Fortune's punishment. Rhodian and Pergamene envoys reported it at Rome in 201, and Roman fear of a combined Hellenistic bloc is one explanation offered for the Second Macedonian War.
scholarship: Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)
Errington, 'The Alleged Syro-Macedonian Pact and the Origins of the Second Macedonian War', Athenaeum 49 (1971)
events.debate: Errington and Magie argued that the pact was Rhodian propaganda; Eckstein argues forcefully that it was real and that it created a 'power-transition crisis' in the Hellenistic system to which Rome reacted.

events.title: Battle of Chios
events.summary: Philip V's fleet was badly mauled off Chios by the combined fleets of Rhodes and Attalus I. Polybius says Philip lost 92 decked ships and 70 lembi, and 9,000 men, far more than his enemies; Attalus was nearly captured. Philip claimed victory because he held the field.
events.detail: Philip then defeated the Rhodians at Lade and ravaged Pergamene territory. Rhodes and Attalus appealed to Rome in autumn 201, setting in motion the Second Macedonian War.

sides.losses: 92 decked ships and 70 lembi lost; 3,000 Macedonians and 6,000 rowers killed (Polybius)

battle.significance: Weakened Macedonian sea power and provoked the appeal to Rome.

events.debate: Polybius' loss figures, from Rhodian sources (Zeno of Rhodes, whom he criticises elsewhere), may be inflated.

events.title: Battle of Panium
events.summary: Antiochus III decisively defeated the Ptolemaic army under the Aetolian mercenary general Scopas at Panium near the sources of the Jordan, using elephants and cataphract cavalry led by his son Antiochus. Coele-Syria and Judaea passed permanently to the Seleucids.
events.detail: Polybius (16.18-19) criticises Zeno of Rhodes' account of the battle. Josephus records Antiochus' charter of privileges to the Jews of Jerusalem, who had welcomed him.

battle.significance: Ended a century of Ptolemaic rule in Coele-Syria and Judaea.

events.title: Rome votes for war with Philip
events.summary: The consul Publius Sulpicius Galba proposed war against Philip V. The comitia centuriata, war-weary after 17 years against Hannibal, rejected it almost unanimously; after a speech by Sulpicius warning that Philip would otherwise invade Italy like Pyrrhus, a second vote approved it. The young envoy Marcus Aemilius Lepidus delivered the ultimatum to Philip at the siege of Abydos.
events.detail: Livy (31.6-8) is the source for the double vote. The ultimatum demanded that Philip make war on no Greek state and submit his disputes with Attalus to arbitration, terms that treated him as a subordinate. The causes of the war are the classic battleground of the imperialism debate: Holleaux saw fear of the Philip-Antiochus pact; Harris aggressive expansionism; Gruen a reluctant Rome drawn in by Greek appeals; Eckstein the systemic crisis of the Hellenistic state system.
scholarship: Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)
Briscoe, A Commentary on Livy XXXI-XXXIII (1973)
Rich, Declaring War in the Roman Republic (1976)
events.debate: Why Rome fought is fiercely debated. Livy's account of the first vote shows that the people did not share the Senate's enthusiasm; Polybius emphasises the Rhodian and Pergamene appeals and Philip's aggression.

events.title: Siege of Abydos
events.summary: Philip V besieged Abydos on the Hellespont. When the walls were breached, the citizens resolved to kill their women and children and burn their property if the city fell; their magistrates surrendered instead, but the populace carried out the mass suicide when Philip entered. Philip gave them three days to die.
events.detail: Polybius (16.30-34) compares the Abydenes to the Phocians and Acarnanians of old. It was here that Marcus Aemilius Lepidus delivered Rome's ultimatum.

sides.strength: citizens of Abydos with Rhodian and Pergamene help

battle.significance: Gave Philip the Straits, but sealed his reputation for savagery in Greek opinion.

events.title: Athens declares war on Philip; Attica ravaged
events.summary: After two Acarnanian youths were executed for straying into the Eleusinian Mysteries, Acarnania and Philip attacked Attica. Athens declared war, abolished the two tribes named after Antigonus and Demetrius and ordered the destruction of all Antigonid statues and inscriptions. Philip ravaged the Attic countryside, burning the Academy, the Lyceum and the sanctuaries and tombs around the city.

events.title: Battle of Cremona
events.summary: Insubres, Boii and Cenomani, led by a Carthaginian officer named Hamilcar who had stayed in Italy, sacked Placentia and besieged Cremona. The praetor Lucius Furius Purpureo crushed them; Hamilcar was killed. Livy claims 35,000 Gauls killed or captured.

sides.strength: praetorian army under L. Furius Purpureo

battle.significance: Opened the final Roman conquest of Cisalpine Gaul.

events.debate: Livy's numbers are typical annalistic exaggeration.

events.title: The Leges Porciae on provocatio
events.summary: One or more laws proposed by members of the Porcian gens extended the citizen's right of appeal (provocatio) against magistrates, in particular protecting Roman citizens from flogging, including outside Rome and in military contexts.
events.detail: Three Porcian laws are mentioned by Cicero (De re publica 2.54). Their authors are usually identified as Publius Porcius Laeca (tribune 199), Cato the Elder (consul 195) and Lucius Porcius Licinus (consul 184). A denarius of P. Laeca (RRC 301/1, c. 110 BC) shows a citizen appealing against a magistrate with the legend PROVOCO.
scholarship: Lintott, 'Provocatio: From the Struggle of the Orders to the Principate', ANRW I.2 (1972)
Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974)
events.debate: Dates, authorship and content are uncertain; the laws are dated anywhere between 199 and 184.

events.title: Battle of the Aous
events.summary: Philip V held the narrow gorge of the Aous (Aoi Stena) for weeks against the new consul Titus Quinctius Flamininus. A shepherd sent by the pro-Roman Epirote chief Charops guided 4,000 Romans over the mountains in three nights to a height above the Macedonian camp; attacked from front and rear, Philip abandoned the pass with the loss of 2,000 men.
events.locName: Aoi Stena, gorge of the Aous (Vjosë) near Këlcyrë

battle.significance: Opened Thessaly to the Romans and brought the Achaeans over to Rome.

events.title: The Achaean League joins Rome
events.summary: At a stormy assembly at Sicyon, the Achaean strategos Aristaenus persuaded the League to abandon its long alliance with Macedon and join Rome. Some cities, including Dyme, Megalopolis and Argos, walked out; Argos then handed itself to Philip, who gave it to Nabis of Sparta.

events.title: Conference of Nicaea
events.summary: Flamininus and Philip negotiated on the shore of the Malian Gulf near Nicaea, Philip speaking from the prow of his ship. Flamininus arranged that the matter be referred to the Senate, where his friends ensured negotiations would fail if his command was prorogued, or succeed if he was to be replaced. It was prorogued.
events.detail: Polybius (18.1-12) records the sharp exchanges in detail, including Philip's taunt to the Aetolians about their own conduct. The episode shows a Roman general manipulating war and peace for his own career.
scholarship: Badian, Titus Quinctius Flamininus: Philhellenism and Realpolitik (1970)

events.title: Battle of Cynoscephalae
events.summary: On the misty 'Dog's Head' hills of Thessaly, an encounter battle between Flamininus and Philip V developed piecemeal. Philip's right wing phalanx charged downhill and pushed back the Roman left; Flamininus attacked the Macedonian left as it was still deploying, using elephants, and broke it. An unnamed military tribune then took 20 maniples from the victorious Roman right and attacked the rear of the Macedonian right phalanx, which collapsed. Macedonian soldiers raising their sarissas in surrender were cut down by Romans who did not understand the signal.
events.detail: Polybius (18.18-27) gives the battle in detail and follows it (18.28-32) with his famous comparison of legion and phalanx: the phalanx is irresistible on level ground and from the front but inflexible, while the legion can fight anywhere and in any formation. Each army numbered about 25,000. The Macedonians lost 8,000 killed and 5,000 captured, the Romans 700. The Aetolian cavalry played a part, and their claim to the victory infuriated Flamininus.

sides.strength: c. 26,000 incl. 6,000 Aetolians and Athamanians, 20 elephants

battle.significance: Ended the Second Macedonian War; Polybius' showcase for the superiority of the legion over the phalanx.

scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius II (1967)
Hammond, 'The Campaign and the Battle of Cynoscephalae in 197 BC', JHS 108 (1988)
events.debate: Livy (33.10) notes that Valerius Antias claimed 40,000 Macedonian dead and Claudius Quadrigarius 32,000, while he himself follows Polybius' 8,000, an explicit example of Livy correcting annalistic inflation with Polybius. The battlefield's exact location is debated.

events.title: Two Spanish provinces and six praetors
events.summary: The number of praetors was raised to six so that two could be sent annually to govern Hispania Citerior (the east coast north of New Carthage) and Hispania Ulterior (the Baetis valley), with boundaries fixed by the praetors of that year.
events.detail: The decision marks Rome's commitment to permanent rule in Spain, motivated in part by silver and by the need to suppress constant warfare. It was followed immediately by a great revolt. Livy (32.28.11) says the praetors were ordered to fix the boundary.
scholarship: Richardson, Hispaniae: Spain and the Development of Roman Imperialism, 218-82 BC (1986)

events.title: Revolt in Spain; death of Sempronius Tuditanus
events.summary: Most of southern and eastern Spain rose against Roman rule, the Turdetani under the chieftain Culchas and the cities of Malaca and Sexi among them. The praetor of Citerior, Gaius Sempronius Tuditanus, was defeated and died of his wounds.

events.title: Battle of the Mincius
events.summary: The consul Gaius Cornelius Cethegus defeated the Insubres and Cenomani on the Mincius after secretly persuading the Cenomani to change sides during the battle. The Carthaginian Hamilcar was captured (in one version) and Cethegus triumphed.

sides.strength: consular army under C. Cornelius Cethegus

battle.significance: Broke the Insubrian coalition; the Cenomani became loyal allies.

events.debate: Livy reports that Hamilcar had already been killed at Cremona in 200 according to other sources.

events.title: Flamininus proclaims the freedom of the Greeks
events.summary: At the Isthmian Games of 196, a herald announced that the Senate and Flamininus declared free, ungarrisoned, untaxed and governed by their own laws the Greek peoples formerly subject to Philip. The crowd's shouts were so loud, Plutarch says, that crows flying overhead fell stunned into the stadium.
events.detail: The peace terms (Polybius 18.44): Philip evacuated all Greek cities in Europe and Asia, surrendered his fleet except five ships and the royal 'sixteen', paid 1,000 talents (half at once) and sent his son Demetrius as a hostage. Whether 'freedom' was sincere philhellenism, propaganda directed at Antiochus, or a Roman form of patronage (libertas under Roman fides) is a central question of the period; the 'fetters of Greece' (Demetrias, Chalcis, Acrocorinth) were evacuated in 194.
scholarship: Badian, Titus Quinctius Flamininus: Philhellenism and Realpolitik (1970)
Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Dmitriev, The Greek Slogan of Freedom and Early Roman Politics in Greece (2011)
events.debate: Badian saw Realpolitik behind philhellenism; Gruen stressed Roman adoption of Greek diplomatic language; Dmitriev traces the slogan's Hellenistic precedents.

events.title: Conference of Lysimachia
events.summary: Roman commissioners met Antiochus III at Lysimachia in Thrace, which he was rebuilding, and told him to keep his hands off the autonomous cities of Asia and out of Europe. Antiochus replied that Asia was none of Rome's business, any more than he meddled in Italy, and that Thrace was his by inheritance from Seleucus I's victory over Lysimachus.
events.detail: The exchange (Polybius 18.49-52) frames the cold war that turned hot in 192. Rumours of Ptolemy V's death broke up the meeting.
scholarship: Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochus the Great (2002)

events.title: Creation of the tresviri epulones
events.summary: A law of the tribune Gaius Licinius Lucullus created a new priestly college of three epulones to organise the sacred banquet (epulum Iovis) at the Ludi Romani and Plebeii, relieving the overburdened pontiffs. It became one of the four great colleges (later septemviri).

events.title: Repeal of the Lex Oppia
events.summary: Two tribunes, Marcus Fundanius and Lucius Valerius, proposed repealing the wartime Lex Oppia. Roman women filled the streets and the approaches to the Forum to lobby men for repeal, the first recorded women's demonstration in Rome. The consul Cato spoke against; the law was repealed.
events.detail: Livy (34.1-8) gives Cato a speech on the dangers of female luxury and assertiveness and Valerius a reply; both speeches are Livy's own compositions and reflect Augustan concerns with moral legislation. The episode is a key text in the history of Roman women.
events.debate: The speeches are Livy's invention; whether Cato really spoke is uncertain.

events.title: Cato in Spain: the battle of Emporiae
events.summary: The consul Cato landed at Emporiae with two legions, sent away his ships to force his men to fight, and defeated a large Iberian army in a dawn attack, using his reserve to break the enemy centre. He then disarmed the tribes north of the Ebro and, by sending sealed letters to all cities to be opened the same day, had their walls demolished simultaneously.
events.detail: Cato boasted that he had taken more towns than he had spent days in Spain (Plutarch). His speeches and the Origines were Livy's sources and are full of self-praise; he also organised the taxation of the iron and silver mines, a major source of Roman revenue.

sides.strength: 2 legions, allies and Spanish auxiliaries, c. 25,000

battle.significance: Pacified north-east Spain; Cato triumphed in 194.

events.debate: Livy (34.15.9) notes that Valerius Antias put the enemy dead at 40,000; Cato's own self-aggrandising account is the ultimate source.

events.title: War against Nabis: siege of Sparta
events.summary: A Panhellenic coalition led by Flamininus, with Achaeans, Macedonians, Rhodians and Pergamenes, took Gythium and attacked Sparta itself. Nabis, whose revolutionary regime had freed helots and redistributed land, sued for peace: he kept Sparta but surrendered Argos and the coastal towns, his fleet and hostages.
events.detail: Livy (34.22-41) presents Nabis as a tyrant; Polybius (13.6-8) tells of his 'Apega', an iron maiden built in the likeness of his wife. Flamininus' moderation in leaving Nabis in place angered the Achaeans and Philopoemen.

battle.significance: Freed Argos but left Nabis in power.

events.debate: Hostile sources dominate the image of Nabis; modern scholars see a social reformer in the line of Agis and Cleomenes.

events.title: Hannibal's suffeteship and flight
events.summary: Elected suffete in 196, Hannibal broke the power of the oligarchic court of 104 judges by making membership annual and reformed the state finances so that the Roman indemnity could be paid without extra taxes. His enemies denounced him at Rome for plotting with Antiochus; when a Roman embassy arrived in 195 he fled by night to Tyre and then to Antiochus at Ephesus.

events.title: Eight citizen colonies on the coasts of southern Italy
events.summary: Rome planted eight citizen colonies of 300 families each at Puteoli, Volturnum, Liternum, Salernum, Buxentum, Sipontum, Tempsa and Croton, on land confiscated from communities that had sided with Hannibal.
events.detail: Puteoli grew into the greatest port of Italy within a century. Several of these small colonies failed, and Sipontum and Buxentum were reported deserted by 186 (Livy 39.23).

events.title: Flamininus' triumph and Roman withdrawal from Greece
events.summary: Flamininus evacuated the last Roman garrisons from Greece, including Acrocorinth, Chalcis and Demetrias, and celebrated a three-day triumph displaying Macedonian armour, bronze and marble statues, silver and gold, including 14,514 gold coins called Philippei. Freed Roman captives sold as slaves in Greece after Cannae, ransomed by the Achaeans, marched behind his chariot with shaved heads.
events.detail: Flamininus had gold staters struck in Greece with his own portrait, the first living Roman on a coin. Greek cities created cults for him with Roma.
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974)

events.title: Lex Sempronia extends usury limits to allies
events.summary: Because Roman creditors evaded the limits on interest by lending through Latin and Italian allies not bound by Roman law, a plebiscite of the tribune Marcus Sempronius Tuditanus applied Roman laws on loans to dealings with allies.

events.title: Emporium and Porticus Aemilia
events.summary: The curule aediles Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Lucius Aemilius Paullus built an emporium on the Tiber below the Aventine and a vast portico outside the Porta Trigemina; the Porticus Aemilia was rebuilt in concrete in 174, one of the earliest large concrete structures.
events.detail: Remains in the Testaccio district, about 487 m long, have traditionally been identified as the Porticus Aemilia, though some argue they belong to the Navalia (ship sheds).
events.debate: Identification of the Testaccio ruins with the Porticus Aemilia has been challenged (Navalia hypothesis).

events.title: Battle of Mutina
events.summary: The consul Lucius Cornelius Merula fought a hard battle against the Boii near Mutina, claiming 14,000 Gauls killed. His legates accused him of letting the enemy escape and blocked his triumph.

sides.strength: consular army under L. Cornelius Merula

battle.significance: Part of the grinding final war against the Boii.

events.title: Latin colonies at Copia (Thurii) and Vibo Valentia
events.summary: Rome founded Latin colonies at Thurii, renamed Copia (193), and at Hipponium, renamed Vibo Valentia (192), in the Bruttian south, the last Latin colonies in southern Italy.

events.title: Murder of Nabis; Sparta joins the Achaean League
events.summary: The Aetolians, seeking to seize Sparta as a base for Antiochus, sent Alexamenus with 1,000 men as 'allies'; he murdered Nabis during a review. The Spartans rose and killed the Aetolians, and Philopoemen brought Sparta into the Achaean League.

events.title: Antiochus III lands at Demetrias
events.summary: Invited by the Aetolians, who named him their commander and 'liberator of Greece', Antiochus crossed to Demetrias in autumn 192 with only 10,000 foot, 500 horse and 6 elephants. Rome declared war. Antiochus wintered at Chalcis, where he married a young Chalcidian woman, which Roman tradition mocked as idleness.
events.detail: Hannibal, at Antiochus' court, urged an attack on Italy itself with a fleet, but was distrusted. The small force suggests Antiochus expected a negotiated outcome or mass Greek defections, neither of which came.
scholarship: Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochus the Great (2002)

events.title: Battle of Thermopylae
events.summary: Antiochus fortified the pass of Thermopylae against the consul Manius Acilius Glabrio, leaving Aetolians to hold the mountain paths. Cato, as a legate, led a force by night over the heights of Callidromus, surprised the Aetolian guard and appeared above Antiochus' camp. The Seleucid army broke; Antiochus fled to Chalcis with 500 men and sailed for Asia.
events.detail: Cato's self-glorifying account (Plutarch, Cato 13-14) was Livy's source; it echoes Persian outflanking of Leonidas in 480.

sides.losses: almost the whole army, according to Livy

battle.significance: Drove Antiochus out of Europe after a single campaign.

events.title: Siege of Heraclea Trachinia
events.summary: After Thermopylae, Acilius Glabrio besieged and stormed the Aetolian stronghold of Heraclea near Mount Oeta, then besieged Naupactus until Flamininus arranged a truce.

events.title: The Aetolians and the meaning of deditio
events.summary: Aetolian envoys led by Phaeneas agreed to entrust themselves to the 'faith of the Romans' (in fidem). When Acilius then demanded the surrender of individuals and threatened to put the envoys in chains, Phaeneas protested that this was not Greek custom. Acilius replied that by Roman usage those who gave themselves into Roman fides were at Rome's absolute disposal.
events.detail: Polybius (20.9-10) uses the scene to explain the gulf between the Greek understanding of pistis as a reciprocal relationship and the Roman deditio in fidem as unconditional surrender. It is a central text for Roman diplomatic concepts.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Eckstein, 'Glabrio and the Aetolians: A Note on Deditio', TAPA 125 (1995)

events.title: Battle of Corycus
events.summary: The Roman fleet of Gaius Livius Salinator, with Eumenes II of Pergamon, defeated the Seleucid admiral Polyxenidas off Cape Corycus near Erythrae, sinking 10 and capturing 13 ships.

battle.significance: Gave the allies the initiative in the Aegean.

events.title: Final defeat of the Boii
events.summary: The consul Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica defeated the Boii in a great battle and forced their surrender, confiscating half their territory for Roman colonists. Livy claims 28,000 Boii killed. Nasica's triumph, opposed by a tribune, was granted; its spoils included 1,471 gold torques.
events.detail: The submission of the Boii ended Gallic independence south of the Po. Strabo (5.1.6) says the Boii were expelled and migrated to the Danube, but the Po valley names and archaeology show many remained under Roman rule.

battle.significance: Completed the Roman conquest of Cisalpine Gaul south of the Po.

events.debate: Strabo's claim of total expulsion of the Boii is contradicted by later evidence.

events.title: Dedication of the temple of Magna Mater
events.summary: The praetor Marcus Junius Brutus dedicated the temple of the Great Mother on the Palatine, thirteen years after the goddess's arrival. Plautus' comedy Pseudolus was staged at the dedication games, as its production notice (didascalia) records.
events.detail: Excavations on the Palatine have found terracotta figurines of Attis in the temple's earliest deposits, showing the Phrygian cult was present from the start.

events.title: Battle of the Eurymedon (Side)
events.summary: A Rhodian fleet under Eudamus defeated the Seleucid Phoenician fleet commanded by Hannibal and Apollonius off Side in Pamphylia. It was Hannibal's only recorded naval command, and his defeat prevented the Phoenician squadrons from joining the main Seleucid fleet.

battle.significance: Kept the Phoenician fleet out of the Aegean.

events.title: Battle of Myonessus
events.summary: The Roman praetor Lucius Aemilius Regillus with Rhodian allies defeated Polyxenidas off Myonessus near Teos. The Rhodian fire-pots, braziers slung on poles from the bows, were decisive. The Seleucids lost 42 ships, and Antiochus abandoned Lysimachia, leaving the Hellespont open.

sides.strength: 58 Roman and 22 Rhodian ships under L. Aemilius Regillus

battle.significance: Gave Rome command of the Aegean and allowed the Scipios to cross into Asia unopposed.

events.title: Antiochus' peace offer and Africanus' son
events.summary: As the Scipios crossed into Asia, Antiochus offered to pay half the Roman war costs and abandon Lampsacus, Smyrna and Alexandria Troas, and offered Africanus, through the envoy Heraclides, the return without ransom of his captured son. Africanus refused to treat but advised Antiochus not to fight. The king returned the son anyway.

events.title: Battle of Magnesia
events.summary: On the plain near Magnesia-ad-Sipylum, Lucius Cornelius Scipio, with Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus effectively in command while Africanus lay ill at Elaea, defeated Antiochus III's huge multi-ethnic army. Eumenes II's light troops stampeded the scythed chariots back into the Seleucid left, and his cavalry broke it. Antiochus' cataphracts on the right routed a Roman legion and charged to the Roman camp, but too late; the Seleucid phalanx, attacked on all sides and disordered by its own panicking elephants, was destroyed.
events.detail: Livy (37.38-44, from Polybius) catalogues the Seleucid army: 16,000 phalangites in ten blocks with elephants between, cataphracts, Galatians, Arab camel-archers, Cretans, Cappadocians and others, 72,000 in all. Livy gives Seleucid losses as 50,000 foot and 3,000 horse and Roman losses as 300 foot, 24 horse and 25 of Eumenes' men, figures many scholars consider propaganda. The date fell in December 190 or January 189 by the Roman calendar, which was then several weeks ahead of the seasons.

sides.strength: c. 30,000 (4 legions and allies, Pergamenes, Achaeans) plus 16 African elephants
c. 72,000 (Livy) with 54 Indian elephants and scythed chariots
sides.losses: 50,000 foot, 3,000 horse killed, 1,400 captured (Livy; probably inflated)

battle.significance: Destroyed Seleucid power west of the Taurus and made Rome the arbiter of the whole Hellenistic world.

scholarship: Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochus the Great (2002)
Bar-Kochva, The Seleucid Army (1976)
Briscoe, A Commentary on Livy XXXIV-XXXVII (1981)
events.debate: Seleucid numbers and losses are disputed; Bar-Kochva accepts Livy's order of battle (from Polybius) but not the loss figures. The role of Domitius is attested by Livy; Africanus' absence spared him the risk of a defeat.

events.title: Decree of Aemilius Paullus at Lascuta
events.summary: On 19 January 189 Lucius Aemilius Paullus, as propraetor in Hispania Ulterior, decreed that the 'slaves of the Hastenses' living in the Turris Lascutana should be free and keep the land and town they held, as long as the Roman people and Senate wished.
events.detail: The bronze tablet, found near Alcalá de los Gazules (Cádiz) and now in the Louvre (CIL II 5041 = ILS 15), is the oldest Latin document from Spain and the oldest original Roman magisterial decree to survive. It shows a governor intervening in local dependency relations to break the power of a hostile city.
events.locName: Turris Lascutana (near Alcalá de los Gazules)

events.title: Siege of Ambracia
events.summary: The consul Marcus Fulvius Nobilior besieged Ambracia, formerly Pyrrhus' capital. When the Romans dug a mine, the defenders countermined and drove them out by filling the tunnel with smoke from burning feathers blown with a bellows. The city surrendered on terms; Fulvius removed its statues and paintings, including statues of the Muses, which he set up in his temple of Hercules Musarum in Rome.
events.detail: Polybius (21.27-28) describes the mine warfare in detail. Ennius accompanied Fulvius and wrote a play, Ambracia, on the campaign, which Cato attacked as unseemly. The Senate later ruled that the looting had been improper.

battle.significance: Forced the Aetolians to accept peace.

events.title: Peace with the Aetolian League: the maiestas clause
events.summary: The Aetolians made peace on harsh terms: an indemnity of 500 talents, surrender of hostages and of the cities taken by Rome since 192, and the obligation to 'preserve the empire and majesty of the Roman people' and to have the same friends and enemies. It was the first Roman treaty with a Greek state to contain the maiestas clause.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)

events.title: Manlius Vulso's Galatian war: Mount Olympus
events.summary: Without clear authorisation from the Senate, the consul Gnaeus Manlius Vulso marched against the Galatians, Antiochus' allies. He stormed the Tolistobogii on their refuge of Mount Olympus with massed slingers and archers, then defeated the Tectosages on Mount Magaba near Ancyra. Livy claims 40,000 captives.
events.detail: Polybius (21.38) tells the story of Chiomara, wife of a Galatian chief, who had a Roman centurion who had raped her beheaded and brought his head to her husband. Manlius' campaign was criticised at Rome as private war for plunder.

battle.significance: Crushed Galatian raiding power and handed Eumenes a secure kingdom; brought vast booty to Rome.

events.title: Latin colony at Bononia
events.summary: A Latin colony of 3,000 settlers was founded at Bononia (Bologna) on land taken from the Boii; cavalrymen received 70 iugera, others 50.

events.title: Treaty of Apamea
events.summary: Antiochus III gave up all territory west of the Taurus, paid 15,000 talents (the largest indemnity in ancient history), surrendered his elephants and all warships but ten, which were not to sail west of Cape Sarpedon, and gave 20 hostages including his son Antiochus. He also had to hand over Hannibal and other enemies of Rome, who escaped.
events.detail: The commissioners of ten under Manlius Vulso divided the territory: Eumenes II received most of Asia Minor north of the Maeander, Rhodes received Lycia and Caria south of the river; Greek cities that had backed Rome were declared free. Rome took no territory, a sign of its preferred style of hegemony through client states.
scholarship: Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)
Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochus the Great (2002)

events.title: Full citizenship for Formiae, Fundi and Arpinum
events.summary: A tribunician law gave Formiae, Fundi and Arpinum, communities of citizens without the vote (cives sine suffragio), full voting citizenship, enrolling them in the tribes Aemilia and Cornelia. Arpinum later produced Marius and Cicero.
